claim: The study analyzed MRI and clinical data from 232 PD patients and 117 controls from the Parkinson's Progression Markers Initiative.
source: We mapped the distribution of atrophy in Parkinson's disease (PD) using magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and clinical data from 232 PD patients and 117 controls from the Parkinson's Progression Markers Initiative.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the sample sizes and data source in the abstract.

claim: Deformation-based morphometry and independent component analysis identified PD-specific atrophy in the midbrain, basal ganglia, basal forebrain, medial temporal lobe, and discrete cortical regions.
source: Deformation-based morphometry and independent component analysis identified PD-specific atrophy in the midbrain, basal ganglia, basal forebrain, medial temporal lobe, and discrete cortical regions.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the brain regions showing atrophy as identified by the analytical methods used.

claim: The degree of atrophy reflected clinical measures of disease severity.
source: The degree of atrophy reflected clinical measures of disease severity.
evidence: The abstract states a correlation between atrophy and clinical severity measures.

claim: The spatial pattern of atrophy demonstrated overlap with intrinsic networks present in healthy brain, as derived from functional MRI.
source: The spatial pattern of atrophy demonstrated overlap with intrinsic networks present in healthy brain, as derived from functional MRI.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the overlap between atrophy patterns and healthy brain networks.

claim: The degree of atrophy in each brain region reflected its functional and anatomical proximity to a presumed disease epicenter in the substantia nigra.
source: Moreover, the degree of atrophy in each brain region reflected its functional and anatomical proximity to a presumed disease epicenter in the substantia nigra, compatible with a trans-neuronal spread of the disease.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the relationship between atrophy and proximity to the substantia nigra.

claim: The results support a network-spread mechanism in PD.
source: These results support a network-spread mechanism in PD.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this conclusion based on the findings.

claim: The atrophy pattern in PD was also seen in healthy aging.
source: Finally, the atrophy pattern in PD was also seen in healthy aging, where it also correlated with the loss of striatal dopaminergic innervation.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states that the PD atrophy pattern is observed in healthy aging.

claim: In healthy aging, the atrophy pattern correlated with the loss of striatal dopaminergic innervation.
source: Finally, the atrophy pattern in PD was also seen in healthy aging, where it also correlated with the loss of striatal dopaminergic innervation.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this correlation in healthy aging subjects.

claim: Parkinson's disease is the second most common neurodegenerative illness.
source: Parkinson's disease (PD) is the second most common neurodegenerative illness.
evidence: The introduction states this as established knowledge.

claim: The clinical hallmarks of PD are due to loss of dopamine neurons in the substantia nigra.
source: Its clinical hallmarks are due to loss of dopamine neurons in the substantia nigra (SN); however, post-mortem studies have shown that PD pathology affects several other brain areas (Goedert et al., 2013).
evidence: The introduction states this as established knowledge with citation.

claim: Post-mortem studies have shown that PD pathology affects several other brain areas beyond the substantia nigra.
source: Its clinical hallmarks are due to loss of dopamine neurons in the substantia nigra (SN); however, post-mortem studies have shown that PD pathology affects several other brain areas (Goedert et al., 2013).
evidence: The introduction cites post-mortem studies showing widespread pathology.

claim: MRI studies have failed to consistently demonstrate regional brain atrophy in the earlier stages of PD.
source: Surprisingly, however, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) studies have failed to consistently demonstrate regional brain atrophy at least in the earlier stages of the disease.
evidence: The introduction states this as a known limitation of prior MRI studies.

claim: The inconsistency in MRI findings is possibly due to small sample sizes, insensitive methodological tools, and lack of statistical power.
source: This is possibly due to studies consisting mostly of small numbers of subjects from single centers and the use of methodological tools that are relatively insensitive to subcortical atrophy, coupled with univariate methods that suffer from lack of statistical power.
evidence: The introduction provides this as a speculative explanation for prior inconsistent findings.

claim: Braak et al. proposed that a disease process spreads from the brainstem to subcortical areas and then to the cerebral hemispheres along neuronal pathways.
source: The distribution of Lewy body pathology in post-mortem samples led Braak et al. to propose that a disease process spreads from the brainstem to subcortical areas and then to the cerebral hemispheres along neuronal pathways (Braak et al., 2003, 2006; Goedert et al., 2013).
evidence: The introduction cites Braak's hypothesis about disease spread.

claim: The network-spread hypothesis suggests that all neurodegenerative diseases target spatially distributed intrinsic brain networks.
source: More generally, the network-spread hypothesis suggests that all neurodegenerative diseases target spatially distributed intrinsic brain networks (Warren et al., 2013).
evidence: The introduction cites the general network-spread hypothesis.

claim: Neurodegenerative diseases are thought to involve prion-like spread of toxic misfolded protein aggregates.
source: At a molecular level, neurodegenerative diseases are now thought to involve prion-like spread of toxic misfolded protein aggregates (Frost and Diamond, 2010; Jucker and Walker, 2013).
evidence: The introduction cites the prion-like spread hypothesis.

claim: Alpha-synuclein fibrils have been shown to spread from cell to cell via neuronal pathways after inoculation in mouse brain.
source: Alpha-synuclein fibrils, implicated in PD pathogenesis, have recently been shown to spread from cell to cell via neuronal pathways after inoculation in mouse brain (Luk et al., 2012; Masuda-Suzukake et al., 2013).
evidence: The introduction cites experimental evidence from mouse studies.

claim: Intrinsic connectivity networks are consistent across studies, in test-retest analysis, and during both rest and task states.
source: Neuroimaging studies have revealed that the spatiotemporal organization of the brain takes the form of intrinsic connectivity networks (ICNs) (Fox and Raichle, 2007; Smith et al., 2009), which are consistent across studies, in test–retest analysis, and during both rest and task states (Damoiseaux et al., 2006; Smith et al., 2009; Zuo et al., 2010).
evidence: The introduction cites studies demonstrating the consistency of ICNs.

claim: Intrinsic networks have been thought to be potential targets for AD since the earliest reports of default mode network dysfunction in the disease.
source: Intrinsic networks have also been thought to be potential targets for AD since the earliest reports of default mode network dysfunction in the disease (Greicius et al., 2004), and analysis of large MRI data sets in AD and other dementias have supported the network-vulnerability hypothesis (Seeley et al., 2009; Raj et al., 2012; Zhou et al., 2012); however, it has yet to be tested in PD.
evidence: The introduction cites prior work on network vulnerability in AD.

claim: The network-vulnerability hypothesis has been supported by analysis of large MRI data sets in AD and other dementias.
source: Intrinsic networks have also been thought to be potential targets for AD since the earliest reports of default mode network dysfunction in the disease (Greicius et al., 2004), and analysis of large MRI data sets in AD and other dementias have supported the network-vulnerability hypothesis (Seeley et al., 2009; Raj et al., 2012; Zhou et al., 2012); however, it has yet to be tested in PD.
evidence: The introduction cites studies supporting the network-vulnerability hypothesis in AD and other dementias.

claim: The network-vulnerability hypothesis has not been tested in PD prior to this study.
source: Intrinsic networks have also been thought to be potential targets for AD since the earliest reports of default mode network dysfunction in the disease (Greicius et al., 2004), and analysis of large MRI data sets in AD and other dementias have supported the network-vulnerability hypothesis (Seeley et al., 2009; Raj et al., 2012; Zhou et al., 2012); however, it has yet to be tested in PD.
evidence: The introduction states this as a gap in the literature.

claim: The study analyzed data from newly diagnosed PD patients (n = 232) and an age-matched control group (n = 117) obtained from the PPMI database.
source: Here, we analyzed data from newly diagnosed PD patients (n = 232) and an age-matched control group (n = 117) obtained from the Parkinson's Progression Markers Initiative (PPMI) database (www.ppmi-info.org/data), an observational, multicenter longitudinal study designed to identify PD progression biomarkers (Marek et al., 2011).
evidence: The introduction explicitly states the sample sizes and data source.

claim: The study used deformation-based morphometry (DBM) and tensor probabilistic independent component analysis (ICA) to identify brain regions demonstrating atrophy in early PD.
source: We used deformation-based morphometry (DBM) and tensor probabilistic independent component analysis (ICA) to identify brain regions demonstrating atrophy in early PD.
evidence: The introduction explicitly states the analytical methods used.

claim: The study compared the set of atrophic regions in PD patients to ICNs from young healthy subjects and tested them for spatial overlap.
source: We compared the set of atrophic regions in PD patients to ICNs from young healthy subjects and tested them for spatial overlap.
evidence: The introduction explicitly states this comparison was performed.

claim: The study used resting state functional MRI (fMRI) and diffusion-weighted MRI (DW-MRI) of healthy subjects to define the normal brain connectome.
source: To further investigate the model of disease propagation through brain networks, we used resting state functional MRI (fMRI) and diffusion-weighted MRI (DW-MRI) of healthy subjects to define the normal brain connectome and determined whether the pattern of atrophy in PD was compatible with spread via this network from a presumed disease epicenter in the SN.
evidence: The introduction explicitly states the use of fMRI and DW-MRI to define the connectome.

claim: The study determined whether the pattern of atrophy in PD was compatible with spread via the brain network from a presumed disease epicenter in the SN.
source: To further investigate the model of disease propagation through brain networks, we used resting state functional MRI (fMRI) and diffusion-weighted MRI (DW-MRI) of healthy subjects to define the normal brain connectome and determined whether the pattern of atrophy in PD was compatible with spread via this network from a presumed disease epicenter in the SN.
evidence: The introduction explicitly states this analysis was performed.

claim: DBM is a measure of the change in the shape of each voxel that results from applying non-linear spatial normalization of the entire brain to a standard template.
source: DBM was used as the measure of local brain atrophy. It is a measure of the change in the shape of each voxel that results from applying non-linear spatial normalization of the entire brain to a standard template (Aubert-Broche et al., 2013).
evidence: The Results section defines DBM with citation.

claim: ICA estimated 30 independent components of deformation in the PPMI data set.
source: ICA was conducted on these DBM images using FSL MELODIC software (Beckmann and Smith, 2004). No constraint was imposed on the number of components, and probabilistic ICA estimated 30 independent components of deformation in the PPMI data set (PD patients and controls combined).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states the number of components identified.

claim: PD patients had significantly lower DBM values in one and only one of the 30 deformation components (p = 0.0001 uncorrected, p = 0.003 with Bonferroni correction).
source: In each of these 30 independent components, the average deformation between PD and control groups was compared using an unpaired t-test. PD patients had significantly lower DBM values in one and only one of the 30 deformation components (p = 0.0001 uncorrected, p = 0.003 with Bonferroni correction).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states the statistical finding.

claim: The next spatial component in terms of statistical significance (p = 0.06, uncorrected) consisted of cerebellar areas VIIIA, VIIB, CrusII, and IX known for their involvement in motor and executive function.
source: The next spatial component in terms of statistical significance (p = 0.06, uncorrected) consisted of cerebellar areas VIIIA, VIIB, CrusII, and IX known for their involvement in motor and executive function (Stoodley and Schmahmann, 2009).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding with citation.

claim: None of the other components demonstrated a difference between PD and controls (p > 0.05 uncorrected for all remaining components).
source: None of the other components demonstrated a difference between PD and controls (p > 0.05 uncorrected for all remaining components).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this negative finding.

claim: Ten of the other ICA components demonstrated an effect of age in the entire group.
source: Ten of the other ICA components demonstrated an effect of age in the entire group.
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding.

claim: Three age-related components showed a positive correlation between the component expression and age (meaning increased volume with age) and all three consisted of ventricle or cerebrospinal fluid space enlargement.
source: In three of these, there was a positive correlation between the component expression and age (meaning increased volume with age) and all three consisted of ventricle or cerebrospinal fluid space enlargement (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding with reference to a figure.

claim: Seven age-related components demonstrated a negative correlation (volume loss with age) and consisted of areas of gray or white matter.
source: The other seven age-related components demonstrated a negative correlation (volume loss with age) and consisted of areas of gray or white matter (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding with reference to a figure.

claim: The PD-ICA network demonstrated greater atrophy with increasing age in both PD patients (r = −0.38, p < 10−9) and controls (r = −0.53, p < 10−9).
source: The PD-ICA network also demonstrated greater atrophy with increasing age in both PD patients (r = −0.38, p < 10−9) and controls (r = −0.53, p < 10−9).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this correlation finding.

claim: The PD-ICA network includes all components of the basal ganglia (substantia nigra, subthalamic nucleus, nucleus accumbens, putamen, caudate nucleus, and internal and external globus pallidus).
source: The PD-ICA network includes all components of the basal ganglia (substantia nigra, subthalamic nucleus, nucleus accumbens, putamen, caudate nucleus, and internal and external globus pallidus), the pedunculopontine nucleus, basal forebrain, including bed nucleus of the stria terminalis and an area containing the nucleus basalis of Meynert, the hypothalamus, amygdala, hippocampus, parahippocampal gyrus, and two thalamic regions, the ventrolateral nucleus and pulvinar.
evidence: The Results section explicitly lists the subcortical regions in the PD-ICA network.

claim: The PD-ICA network includes the pedunculopontine nucleus, basal forebrain, hypothalamus, amygdala, hippocampus, parahippocampal gyrus, and two thalamic regions (ventrolateral nucleus and pulvinar).
source: The PD-ICA network includes all components of the basal ganglia (substantia nigra, subthalamic nucleus, nucleus accumbens, putamen, caudate nucleus, and internal and external globus pallidus), the pedunculopontine nucleus, basal forebrain, including bed nucleus of the stria terminalis and an area containing the nucleus basalis of Meynert, the hypothalamus, amygdala, hippocampus, parahippocampal gyrus, and two thalamic regions, the ventrolateral nucleus and pulvinar.
evidence: The Results section explicitly lists these subcortical regions in the PD-ICA network.

claim: Cortical regions in the PD-ICA network include the insula, occipital cortex Brodmann area 19, superior temporal gyrus, rostral anterior cingulate cortex, premotor and supplementary areas, and parts of lateral prefrontal cortex.
source: Cortical regions in this network are the insula, occipital cortex Brodmann area 19, superior temporal gyrus, rostral anterior cingulate cortex, premotor and supplementary areas, and parts of lateral prefrontal cortex (Figure 1, Tables 1, 2; see also Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The Results section explicitly lists the cortical regions with reference to figures and tables.

claim: There was a significant correlation between individual SBR and DBM values in the PD-ICA network in the PD group (r = 0.23, p < 0.0005).
source: There was a significant correlation between individual SBR and DBM values in the PD-ICA network in the PD group (r = 0.23, p < 0.0005, Figure 2).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this correlation finding with reference to a figure.

claim: The greater the loss of dopamine nerve terminals, the greater the volume loss in the PD-ICA network.
source: This shows that the greater the loss of dopamine nerve terminals, the greater the volume loss in the PD-ICA network.
evidence: The Results section explicitly interprets the correlation between SBR and DBM.

claim: There was a significant correlation between SBR and DBM values in the PD-ICA network in the control group (r = 0.33, p < 0.0005).
source: There was also a significant correlation between these two measures in the control group (r = 0.33, p < 0.0005).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this correlation finding in controls.

claim: There was a significant correlation between DBM values within the PD-ICA network and UPDRS III in the PD patients (r = −0.22, p < 0.001).
source: There was a significant correlation between DBM values within the PD-ICA network and UPDRS III in the PD patients (r = −0.22, p < 0.001; Figure 2).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this correlation finding with reference to a figure.

claim: SBR was not significantly correlated with age in the PD subjects (r = −0.10, p = 0.12).
source: SBR was not significantly correlated with age in the PD subjects (r = −0.10, p = 0.12) but it was in controls (r = −0.35, p < 0.0001).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this negative finding.

claim: SBR was significantly correlated with age in controls (r = −0.35, p < 0.0001).
source: SBR was not significantly correlated with age in the PD subjects (r = −0.10, p = 0.12) but it was in controls (r = −0.35, p < 0.0001).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this correlation finding in controls.

claim: In PD subjects, SBR was significantly correlated with UPDRS III (r = 0.20, p = 0.002).
source: Also, in PD subjects, SBR was significantly correlated with UPDRS III (r = 0.20, p = 0.002).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this correlation finding.

claim: There was one other component marginally correlated with disease severity (r = −0.2, p = 0.048, Bonferroni corrected) consisting of cerebellar areas VIIIA, VIIIB, CrusII, and IX.
source: There was only one other component marginally correlated with disease severity (r = −0.2, p = 0.048, Bonferroni corrected) consisting of the previously mentioned cerebellar network, areas VIIIA, VIIIB, CrusII, and IX.
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding.

claim: In the PD group, the model (PD-ICA ~ 1 + Age + UPDRS III + SBR) showed an effect of age (p = 2.4 e−08), UPDRS III (p = 0.06) and SBR (p = 0.01).
source: In the PD group, the model (PD-ICA ~ 1 + Age + UPDRS III + SBR) showed an effect of age (p = 2.4 e−08), UPDRS III (p = 0.06) and SBR (p = 0.01).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states the results of the multiple linear regression.

claim: In the controls, the model (PD-ICA ~ 1 + Age + SBR) demonstrated an effect of age (p = 4.7 e−08) but not SBR (p = 0.17).
source: In the controls, the model (PD-ICA ~ 1 + Age + SBR) demonstrated an effect of age (p = 4.7 e−08) but not SBR (p = 0.17).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states the results of the multiple linear regression in controls.

claim: There was no significant effect of scanning site after correcting for multiple comparisons (p > 0.1).
source: Finally, multivariate analysis was used to look for an effect of scanning site. For each obtained DBM-network, we applied the model: DBM ~ Group (PD/Control) + Age + Gender + Site. There was no significant effect of site after correcting for multiple comparisons (p > 0.1).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this negative finding.

claim: Only two ICA networks passed the threshold of |r| > 0.25 when compared to the resting-state SN seed-based map.
source: First, we compared the resting-state SN seed-based map (Figure 3B) with all 30 structural maps obtained from the PPMI ICA analysis. Only two ICA networks passed the threshold of |r| > 0.25.
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding.

claim: One of the two networks that passed the threshold is mostly white matter areas (r = 0.36), while the other is mostly gray matter areas (r = 0.30).
source: These two networks correspond to very similar subcortical networks in basal ganglia and brainstem, one of which is mostly white matter areas (r = 0.36), while the other is mostly gray matter areas (r = 0.30).
evidence: The Results section explicitly describes these two networks.

claim: The gray matter network that passed the threshold is the PD-ICA network in which atrophy correlated with disease severity.
source: The latter is the aforementioned PD-ICA network in which atrophy correlated with disease severity (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The Results section explicitly identifies this network.

claim: One of the 70 rsfMRI ICNs in normal brain provided by Smith et al. (2009) passed the threshold (with r = 0.32) when compared to the PD-ICA network.
source: Then, we compared the PD-ICA network to the 70 rsfMRI ICNs in normal brain provided by Smith et al. (2009). One of the 70 networks passed the threshold (with r = 0.32).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding with citation.

claim: The ICN that passed the threshold has been related to reward tasks, interoceptive functions, and motor/sensory processing.
source: This network has been related to reward tasks, interoceptive functions, and motor/sensory processing (Figure 3C).
evidence: The Results section explicitly describes the functional associations of this network.

claim: Four components from the 100 resting-state ICNs from the Human Connectome Project showed spatial overlap to the PD-ICA network using spatial correlation.
source: We then repeated this comparison using a finer decomposition of 100 resting-state ICNs from the Human Connectome Project (HCP) (Smith et al., 2013) using MELODIC. Four components showed spatial overlap to the PD-ICA network using spatial correlation (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding with citation and reference to a figure.

claim: The mean fMRI time series from the four HCP components demonstrated significant inter-correlation (p < 0.0016 by permutation testing).
source: The mean fMRI time series from these components were then used to determine whether they themselves belonged to one larger ICN. These time series demonstrated significant inter-correlation (p < 0.0016 by permutation testing).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this statistical finding.

claim: Hierarchical clustering confirmed that all four HCP components clustered together.
source: Finally, hierarchical clustering (Smith et al., 2013) confirmed that all four components clustered together.
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding with citation.

claim: Only one of the 30 networks passed the threshold (r = 0.28) when compared to a map of regions responding to stimulus value during fMRI experiments, namely the PD-ICA network.
source: We also compared the PD-ICA network to a map of regions responding to stimulus value during fMRI experiments as identified by meta-analysis (Bartra et al., 2013). In these experiments, subjects typically evaluated an offered item (say a food) and experimenters identified brain regions where the fMRI signal tracked subjective value (e.g., willingness to pay for the item). The premise is that PD may affect dopamine projection sites that encode aspects of stimulus value. Only one of the 30 networks passed the threshold (r = 0.28), namely the aforementioned PD-ICA network (Figure 3D).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding with citation and reference to a figure.

claim: The PD-ICA network exhibited significant spatial overlap with presumed intrinsic brain networks determined by three different methods.
source: In summary, the PD-ICA network exhibited significant spatial overlap with presumed intrinsic brain networks determined by three different methods.
evidence: The Results section explicitly summarizes this finding.

claim: There was a significant correlation between resting-state functional connectivity of each node with SN (in healthy brain) and the PD-related deformation (PD minus control t-score), (r = 0.40, p < 0.0001).
source: There was a significant correlation between resting-state functional connectivity of each node with SN (in healthy brain) and the PD-related deformation (PD minus control t-score), (r = 0.40, p < 0.0001).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this correlation finding.

claim: The correlation between functional connectivity with SN and PD-related deformation was unchanged (r = 0.38, p < 0.0001) after controlling for Euclidean distance.
source: We repeated the same analysis controlling for spatial proximity between each region and SN by entering Euclidean distance as a covariate. The correlation was unchanged (r = 0.38, p < 0.0001), suggesting that the relationship cannot be explained by spatial proximity.
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding after controlling for spatial proximity.

claim: Higher functional connection between a given region and SN is related to higher PD-related atrophy in that region.
source: The correlation implies that higher functional connection between a given region and SN is related to higher PD-related atrophy in that region (Figure 4).
evidence: The Results section explicitly interprets the correlation finding with reference to a figure.

claim: There was a significant relationship between the level of atrophy of each region and its geodesic distance to the SN (r = −0.28, p < 0.003) when using an anatomical measure of connectivity (DW-MRI).
source: When using an anatomical measure of connectivity (DW-MRI) (Figure 4), we also observed a significant relationship between the level of atrophy of each region and its geodesic distance to the SN (r = −0.28, p < 0.003).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this correlation finding with reference to a figure.

claim: The relationship between atrophy and geodesic distance to SN was not different after controlling for Euclidean distance to SN (r = −0.25, p < 0.005).
source: These results were not different after controlling for Euclidean distance to SN (r = −0.25, p < 0.005).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding after controlling for spatial proximity.

claim: SN was the likeliest disease propagator when using the rsfMRI connectome.
source: Finally, we repeated this analysis using every ROI as a potential disease propagator and found that SN was the likeliest disease propagator when using the rsfMRI connectome (Table 3).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding with reference to a table.

claim: The red nucleus (r = 0.28) and subthalamic nucleus (r = 0.28) were also identified as potential propagators.
source: However, the red nucleus (r = 0.28) and subthalamic nucleus (r = 0.28) were also identified as potential propagators.
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding.

claim: Repeating the propagator analysis using a tractography-derived connectome revealed that the SN was one of the likeliest propagators, but numerous cerebellar regions also emerged as potential propagators.
source: Repeating this analysis using a tractography-derived connectome also revealed that the SN was one of the likeliest propagators, but numerous cerebellar regions also emerged as potential propagators (Figure 4—source data 2).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding.

claim: The emergence of cerebellar regions as potential propagators may be due to difficulty in accurate identification of the targets of brainstem white matter tracts using DW-MRI.
source: This may be due to difficulty in accurate identification of the targets of brainstem white matter tracts using DW-MRI (Ford et al., 2013).
evidence: The Results section provides this as a speculative explanation with citation.

claim: Most MRI studies to date using T1-weighted images in PD have reported normal volumes of brainstem, basal ganglia, and cerebral cortex.
source: Most MRI studies to date using T1-weighted images in PD have reported normal volumes of brainstem, basal ganglia, and cerebral cortex.
evidence: The Discussion section states this as prior knowledge.

claim: In the SN, measurements of volume and shape have been inconclusive, reporting either no change, a decrease, or increase in volume depending on the method used.
source: In the SN, measurements of volume and shape have been inconclusive, reporting either no change, a decrease, or increase in volume depending on the method used (Pyatigorskaya et al., 2014).
evidence: The Discussion section cites prior inconsistent findings.

claim: Most studies using parametric mapping have failed to report a difference in SN.
source: However, most studies using parametric mapping have failed to report a difference in SN.
evidence: The Discussion section states this as prior knowledge.

claim: Reduced putamen or caudate volume has been reported but only in advanced cases with mild cognitive impairment or dementia.
source: Reduced putamen or caudate volume has been reported but only in advanced cases with mild cognitive impairment or dementia (Apostolova et al., 2010; Silbert and Kaye, 2010; Pyatigorskaya et al., 2014).
evidence: The Discussion section cites prior findings in advanced PD.

claim: Hippocampus and amygdala atrophy are typically linked to cognitive impairment in PD.
source: Similarly, hippocampus and amygdala atrophy are typically linked to cognitive impairment (for review see Silbert and Kaye, 2010; Ibarretxe-Bilbao et al., 2011).
evidence: The Discussion section cites prior findings linking these structures to cognitive impairment.

claim: Studies using voxel-based morphometry (VBM), DBM, or cortical thickness measurements have reported significant differences between PD and controls in parahippocampal gyrus, inferior, middle and frontal temporal gyrus, parietal lobe and occipital lobe, but typically in advanced patients with cognitive impairment.
source: With regard to cortical areas, studies using voxel-based morphometry (VBM), DBM, or cortical thickness measurements have reported significant differences between PD and controls in parahippocampal gyrus, inferior, middle and frontal temporal gyrus, parietal lobe and occipital lobe, but, once again, typically in advanced patients with cognitive impairment (Silbert and Kaye, 2010; Ibarretxe-Bilbao et al., 2011; Camicioli, 2013; Pyatigorskaya et al., 2014).
evidence: The Discussion section cites prior findings in advanced PD with cognitive impairment.

claim: The finding of an atrophy network including brainstem and subcortical regions in de novo patients is likely due to the larger number of participants available through the PPMI database compared to previous relatively underpowered investigations.
source: Our finding of an atrophy network including brainstem and subcortical regions in these de novo patients is likely due to the larger number of participants available through the PPMI database compared to previous relatively underpowered investigations.
evidence: The Discussion section provides this as an explanation for the novel findings.

claim: Eidelberg and colleagues were the first to use data reduction techniques (principal component analysis) to map PD pathology using [18F]fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) positron emission tomography.
source: Eidelberg and colleagues (Eidelberg, 2009) were the first to use data reduction techniques (principal component analysis) to map PD pathology using [18F]fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) positron emission tomography.
evidence: The Discussion section cites prior work by Eidelberg.

claim: Eidelberg identified a PD-related pattern (PDRP) implicating globus pallidus, putamen, thalamus, premotor and supplementary motor areas.
source: They identified a PD-related pattern (PDRP) implicating several regions identified in our analysis, namely globus pallidus, putamen, thalamus, premotor and supplementary motor areas.
evidence: The Discussion section describes Eidelberg's findings.

claim: The expression of the PDRP differentiates patients from healthy controls and correlates with measures of disease severity.
source: The expression of this PDRP differentiates patients from healthy controls and correlates with measures of disease severity.
evidence: The Discussion section describes the properties of the PDRP.

claim: The PDRP probably reflects functional effects of the disease more than neuronal atrophy, as evidenced by the fact that it is normalized by levodopa or deep brain stimulation.
source: However, it probably reflects functional effects of the disease more than neuronal atrophy, as evidenced by the fact that it is normalized by levodopa or deep brain stimulation (Eidelberg, 2009).
evidence: The Discussion section provides this interpretation with citation.

claim: The set of regions demonstrating atrophy in the PD group corresponded spatially to one ICN in normal brain.
source: We found that the set of regions demonstrating atrophy in the PD group corresponded spatially to one ICN in normal brain.
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly states this finding.

claim: The PD-ICA set of regions corresponded to a normal ICN identified by seed-based resting-state functional connectivity and ICA.
source: We showed that our PD-ICA set of regions corresponded to a normal ICN identified by seed-based resting-state functional connectivity and ICA (Smith et al., 2009, 2013).
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly states this finding with citations.

claim: The finding that PD targets a set of connected brain regions supports the network-spread hypothesis.
source: The finding that PD targets a set of connected brain regions supports the network-spread hypothesis, although an alternate explanation is that neurons in one network could share a common vulnerability.
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly states this interpretation.

claim: An alternate explanation for the network targeting is that neurons in one network could share a common vulnerability.
source: The finding that PD targets a set of connected brain regions supports the network-spread hypothesis, although an alternate explanation is that neurons in one network could share a common vulnerability.
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly provides this alternative explanation.

claim: The brain regions that make up the PD-ICA network are involved in reward and motivation.
source: The brain regions that make up the PD-ICA network are involved in reward and motivation, as demonstrated by the fact that they respond to the subjective value of a perceived stimulus during fMRI (Bartra et al., 2013).
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly states this functional interpretation with citation.

claim: All the regions of the value network receive projections from midbrain dopamine neurons.
source: All the regions of this value network receive projections from midbrain dopamine neurons, in keeping with this neurotransmitter's role in signaling incentive value (Salamone et al., 2005; Berridge, 2006).
evidence: The Discussion section states this with citations.

claim: Misfolded synuclein fibrils injected focally into rodent brains spread to neuronally connected but not adjacent areas.
source: Misfolded synuclein fibrils injected focally into rodent brains spread to neuronally connected but not adjacent areas (Luk et al., 2012; Masuda-Suzukake et al., 2013) (see also Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The Discussion section cites experimental evidence from rodent studies.

claim: The SN could act as a propagator, since the rate of atrophy in any brain region was proportional to its effective topological distance from the SN, as determined by either functional (rsfMRI) or anatomical (DW-MRI) connectivity.
source: Here, we tried to identify a putative best propagator or epicenter of the disease by creating functional and anatomical connectomes from an anatomical brain atlas. We showed that the SN could act as a propagator, since the rate of atrophy in any brain region was proportional to its effective topological distance from the SN, as determined by either functional (rsfMRI) or anatomical (DW-MRI) connectivity.
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly states this finding.

claim: The Braak scheme identifies the dorsal motor nucleus (DMN) of the vagus in the medulla as the first affected CNS structure.
source: We note that, while the SN contains dopamine neurons whose degeneration accounts for all the key clinical features of early PD, the Braak scheme identifies the dorsal motor nucleus (DMN) of the vagus in the medulla as the first affected CNS structure.
evidence: The Discussion section cites the Braak staging scheme.

claim: Recent evidence supports the potential transfer of pathogenic alpha-synuclein from the intestine to the DMN via the vagus nerve.
source: Indeed, recent evidence supports the potential transfer of pathogenic alpha-synuclein from the intestine to the DMN via the vagus nerve (Holmqvist et al., 2014).
evidence: The Discussion section cites recent evidence for gut-to-brain transfer.

claim: The DMN did not demonstrate atrophy in PD compared to control subjects in the current study.
source: In the current study, the DMN did not demonstrate atrophy in PD compared to control subjects.
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly states this negative finding.

claim: The lack of DMN atrophy may be due to insensitivity of T1-weighted MRI-based anatomical methods in identifying neuronal loss in lower brainstem structures.
source: Perhaps this is due to insensitivity of T1-weighted MRI-based anatomical methods in identifying neuronal loss in lower brainstem structures.
evidence: The Discussion section provides this as a speculative explanation.

claim: The DMN is much smaller than the SN (approximately 1/10–1/20 in volume) and has limited contrast in T1 MRI.
source: The DMN is much smaller that the SN (approximately 1/10–1/20 in volume) and has limited contrast in T1 MRI.
evidence: The Discussion section provides anatomical context for the lack of DMN detection.

claim: The SN could act as the propagator of the disease to the supratentorial CNS.
source: Our results, however, suggest that the SN could act as the propagator of the disease to the supratentorial CNS.
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly states this interpretation.

claim: Spatial resolution limitations for T1-weighted MRI, fMRI, and DW-MRI make it difficult to localize atrophy to small nuclei with complete certainty.
source: Note, however, that spatial resolution limitations for all of the imaging modalities used here, T1-weighted MRI, fMRI, and DW-MRI, make it difficult to localize atrophy to small nuclei with complete certainty.
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly acknowledges this limitation.

claim: Spatial inaccuracy in atlas generation and normalization of subject images to MNI space may compound the problem of localizing atrophy to small structures.
source: Spatial inaccuracy in atlas generation and normalization of subject images to Montreal Neurological Institute (MNI) space may compound this problem.
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly acknowledges this limitation.

claim: The propagator analysis identified SN, subthalamic nucleus, and red nucleus as potential propagators, but the imaging techniques used do not allow full resolution of these structures.
source: This is especially relevant to small structures of the basal forebrain and midbrain. For example, the propagator analysis identified SN, subthalamic nucleus, and red nucleus as potential propagators, but it is clear that the imaging techniques used here do not allow us to fully resolve these structures, either anatomically or functionally.
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly acknowledges this limitation.

claim: Changes in iron accumulation in SN, globus pallidus, or red nucleus may be interpreted as volume changes by the DBM methodology.
source: Furthermore, because T1-weighted MRI is sensitive to iron content, changes in iron accumulation, for example, in SN, globus pallidus, or red nucleus, may be interpreted as volume changes by the DBM methodology.
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly acknowledges this potential confound.

claim: All the areas identified in Braak stage 3 (pedunculopontine nucleus, amygdala, basal forebrain, and substantia nigra) belong to the PD-ICA network.
source: Nonetheless, comparing the atrophy pattern identified here to the stages described by Braak et al. (2003), Braak et al. (2006), we note that all the areas identified in stage 3 (pedunculopontine nucleus, amygdala, basal forebrain, and substantia nigra), stage 4 (temporal mesocortex and hippocampus), and stage 5 (insula, cingulate cortex, and temporal neocortex) belong to our PD-ICA network.
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly compares the findings to Braak staging with citations.

claim: All the areas identified in Braak stage 4 (temporal mesocortex and hippocampus) belong to the PD-ICA network.
source: Nonetheless, comparing the atrophy pattern identified here to the stages described by Braak et al. (2003), Braak et al. (2006), we note that all the areas identified in stage 3 (pedunculopontine nucleus, amygdala, basal forebrain, and substantia nigra), stage 4 (temporal mesocortex and hippocampus), and stage 5 (insula, cingulate cortex, and temporal neocortex) belong to our PD-ICA network.
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly compares the findings to Braak staging with citations.

claim: All the areas identified in Braak stage 5 (insula, cingulate cortex, and temporal neocortex) belong to the PD-ICA network.
source: Nonetheless, comparing the atrophy pattern identified here to the stages described by Braak et al. (2003), Braak et al. (2006), we note that all the areas identified in stage 3 (pedunculopontine nucleus, amygdala, basal forebrain, and substantia nigra), stage 4 (temporal mesocortex and hippocampus), and stage 5 (insula, cingulate cortex, and temporal neocortex) belong to our PD-ICA network.
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly compares the findings to Braak staging with citations.

claim: Braak hypothesized that the medial temporal lobe served as a beachhead for further propagation to the remaining cortex.
source: Braak hypothesized that the medial temporal lobe served as a beachhead for further propagation to the remaining cortex, and interestingly three of the best supratentorial propagators identified here were the parahippocampal gyrus, anterior medial temporal lobe, and hippocampus (Table 3).
evidence: The Discussion section cites Braak's hypothesis.

claim: Three of the best supratentorial propagators identified in this study were the parahippocampal gyrus, anterior medial temporal lobe, and hippocampus.
source: Braak hypothesized that the medial temporal lobe served as a beachhead for further propagation to the remaining cortex, and interestingly three of the best supratentorial propagators identified here were the parahippocampal gyrus, anterior medial temporal lobe, and hippocampus (Table 3).
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly states this finding with reference to a table.

claim: The network-spread model predicts that connectome hubs should be especially vulnerable to disease spread.
source: Another prediction of the network-spread model is that connectome hubs should be especially vulnerable to disease spread (Zhou et al., 2012).
evidence: The Discussion section cites this prediction from the network-spread model.

claim: Hubs are defined as brain regions that are highly connected using graph theoretical metrics such as degree or betweenness.
source: Hubs are defined as brain regions that are highly connected using graph theoretical metrics such as degree (Crossley et al., 2014) or betweenness (He et al., 2009).
evidence: The Discussion section defines hubs with citations.

claim: In a recent meta-analysis, Crossley et al. found that most neurodegenerative diseases, including AD and fronto-temporal dementia, did indeed target hubs, with PD being a salient exception.
source: In a recent meta-analysis, Crossley et al. (2014) found that most neurodegenerative diseases, including AD and fronto-temporal dementia, did indeed target hubs. However, one salient exception was PD.
evidence: The Discussion section cites findings from a meta-analysis.

claim: One possibility for PD not targeting hubs in prior studies is that the PD studies included in the meta-analysis were too small in scale or methodologically incapable of detecting the true extent of damage.
source: One possibility is that the PD studies included in the meta-analysis were too small in scale or methodologically incapable of detecting the true extent of damage.
evidence: The Discussion section provides this as a speculative explanation.

claim: The current study identified numerous hub regions in the PD-ICA network, including the medial temporal lobe, putamen, insula, occipital cortex, anterior cingulate, superior frontal gyrus, and middle frontal gyrus.
source: It is intriguing that our study identified numerous hub regions (Bassett et al., 2008; He et al., 2009; Crossley et al., 2014) in the PD-ICA network, including the medial temporal lobe, putamen, insula, occipital cortex, anterior cingulate, superior frontal gyrus, and middle frontal gyrus.
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly states this finding with citations.

claim: One notable hub region absent from the PD-ICA network is the posterior cingulate gyrus/precuneus, an area typically affected in AD.
source: One notable hub region absent from our PD-ICA network is the posterior cingulate gyrus/precuneus, an area typically affected in AD (Buckner et al., 2009).
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly notes this absence with citation.

claim: The control subjects demonstrated age-related loss of dopamine innervation and atrophy in the PD-ICA network.
source: In sum, the control subjects demonstrated age-related loss of dopamine innervation and atrophy in the PD-ICA network.
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly states this finding.

claim: Healthy aging is associated with a progressive loss of dopamine neurotransmission.
source: It is known that healthy aging is associated with a progressive loss of dopamine neurotransmission (Fearnley and Lees, 1991), and that this may account for motor slowing and executive cognitive impairment that occurs with age (Jagust, 2013).
evidence: The Discussion section cites this as established knowledge.

claim: Loss of dopamine neurotransmission in healthy aging may account for motor slowing and executive cognitive impairment that occurs with age.
source: It is known that healthy aging is associated with a progressive loss of dopamine neurotransmission (Fearnley and Lees, 1991), and that this may account for motor slowing and executive cognitive impairment that occurs with age (Jagust, 2013).
evidence: The Discussion section cites this as established knowledge.

claim: Subtle Parkinsonian signs such as stooped posture, bradykinesia, and reduced facial expression in the healthy elderly were associated with SN neuron loss at post-mortem.
source: Indeed, subtle Parkinsonian signs such as stooped posture, bradykinesia, and reduced facial expression in the healthy elderly were associated with SN neuron loss at post-mortem (Ross et al., 2004).
evidence: The Discussion section cites post-mortem evidence.

claim: Neurodegeneration of the extended dopamine network occurs in healthy aging, albeit without attaining the severity of outright PD.
source: Our results extend these findings by showing that neurodegeneration of the extended dopamine network also occurs in healthy aging, albeit without attaining the severity of outright PD, possibly via loss of neurotrophism, or perhaps, due to low-level mitochondrial dysfunction or synucleinopathy (Olanow and Brundin, 2013).
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly states this interpretation with citation.

claim: PD might target the PD-ICA network due to a dual hit effect of pathology superimposed upon normal aging.
source: PD might then target the PD-ICA network due to a dual hit effect of pathology superimposed upon normal aging.
evidence: The Discussion section provides this as a speculative explanation.

claim: Patients included in this study were diagnosed on average 7 months prior to the investigation.
source: Patients included in this study were diagnosed on average 7 months prior to the investigation and had no evidence of dementia (Table 4).
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly states the disease duration.

claim: Patients included in this study had no evidence of dementia.
source: Patients included in this study were diagnosed on average 7 months prior to the investigation and had no evidence of dementia (Table 4).
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly states the cognitive status with reference to a table.

claim: The PPMI is an observational, multicenter longitudinal study designed to identify PD progression biomarkers.
source: The PPMI is described at www.ppmi-info.org. PPMI is a public–private partnership funded by the Michael J Fox Foundation for Parkinson's Research and funding partners listed at www.ppmi-info.org/fundingpartners. It is an observational, multicenter longitudinal study designed to identify PD biomarkers (Marek et al., 2011).
evidence: The Materials and methods section describes the PPMI study with citation.

claim: MRI data were acquired in 16 centers participating in the PPMI project, using scanners from three different manufacturers (GE medical systems, Siemens, and Philips medical systems).
source: MRI data were acquired in 16 centers participating in the PPMI project, using scanners from three different manufacturers (GE medical systems, Siemens, and Philips medical systems).
evidence: The Materials and methods section explicitly states the data acquisition details.

claim: In total data from 355 subjects (237 PD patients and 118 age-matched controls) were used.
source: In total data from 355 subjects (237 PD patients and 118 age-matched controls) were used.
evidence: The Materials and methods section explicitly states the total sample size.

claim: Six subjects, five PD patients and one age-matched control, were excluded from analysis due to failure in MRI processing.
source: Six subjects, five PD patients and one age-matched control, were excluded from analysis due to failure in MRI processing.
evidence: The Materials and methods section explicitly states the exclusions.

claim: rsfMRI was acquired in 51 healthy, right-handed volunteers (mean age: 23.6 ± 5.9, range: 18–47, 32 men, 63%).
source: We acquired rsfMRI in 51 healthy, right-handed volunteers (mean age: 23.6 ± 5.9, range: 18–47, 32 men, 63%).
evidence: The Materials and methods section explicitly states the rsfMRI sample characteristics.

claim: The Illinois Institute of Technology Human Brain Atlas v.3 contains structural (T1) and high angular resolution DW-MRI data from 72 human subjects.
source: To obtain white matter connectivity maps of normal brain, we used the Illinois Institute of Technology Human Brain Atlas v.3 (Varentsova et al., 2014) (http://www.nitrc.org/projects/iit2/). This atlas contains structural (T1) and high angular resolution DW-MRI data, and probabilistic gray matter maps of the adult human brain in MNI space. The atlas was generated from MRI data from 72 human subjects (42 females (59%): mean age 26.6 ± 4.8 years, range 20–39 years; 30 males: mean age 31.9 ± 4.9 years, range 22–40 years).
evidence: The Materials and methods section explicitly describes the atlas with citation.

claim: VBM does not preserve the entirety of the MRI data.
source: We decided against VBM as it does not preserve the entirety of the MRI data, and there is some suggestion that it is less sensitive than DBM to subcortical atrophy (Borghammer et al., 2010; Scanlon et al., 2011).
evidence: The Materials and methods section provides this as a rationale for not using VBM.

claim: There is some suggestion that VBM is less sensitive than DBM to subcortical atrophy.
source: We decided against VBM as it does not preserve the entirety of the MRI data, and there is some suggestion that it is less sensitive than DBM to subcortical atrophy (Borghammer et al., 2010; Scanlon et al., 2011).
evidence: The Materials and methods section cites this as a reason for choosing DBM over VBM.

claim: ICA is a statistical method to decompose multivariate data into statistically independent components.
source: We used ICA to extract patterns of deformation in PD patients and age-matched controls. ICA is a statistical method to decompose multivariate data into statistically independent components (Calhoun et al., 2001; Beckmann and Smith, 2004; Hyvärinen et al., 2004).
evidence: The Materials and methods section defines ICA with citations.

claim: MELODIC applies an initial principal component analysis-based dimension estimation to find the optimal number of independent components.
source: MELODIC applies an initial principal component analysis-based dimension estimation to find the optimal number of independent components and then uses this number in the decomposition procedure to identify the independent spatial components.
evidence: The Materials and methods section describes the MELODIC algorithm.

claim: The ICA algorithm in MELODIC is sensitive to sparsely distributed (super-Gaussian) data as typically seen in fMRI.
source: The ICA algorithm in MELODIC is sensitive to sparsely distributed (super-Gaussian) data (Daubechies et al., 2009) as typically seen in fMRI.
evidence: The Materials and methods section describes the properties of the MELODIC algorithm with citation.

claim: The DBM data used in this study possessed the super-Gaussian property (kurtosis >4).
source: We confirmed that the DBM data used here possessed this super-Gaussian property (kurtosis >4).
evidence: The Materials and methods section explicitly states this data property was confirmed.

claim: Spatial cross-correlation (Pearson) was used as the measure of similarity between spatial maps.
source: Spatial cross-correlation (Pearson) was used as the measure of similarity.
evidence: The Materials and methods section explicitly states the similarity metric used.

claim: |r| > 0.25 was chosen as indicative of similarity between two spatial maps as this has been argued to guard against false positives in similar comparisons between ICA-derived spatial maps.
source: We chose |r| > 0.25 as indicative of similarity between two spatial maps as this has been argued to guard against false positives in a similar comparison between ICA-derived spatial maps (Smith et al., 2009).
evidence: The Materials and methods section justifies the threshold choice with citation.
